lesson.menu_desc: Phase 3 -- noun clauses, for building an opinion that holds -- 34 slides
lesson.subtitle: Lesson 27 -- What Matters Is... -- Noun Clauses for Opinions
lesson.title_tag: Professor View -- Mark Kazuyoshi Seki Omagari | Lesson 27 -- What Matters Is...
lesson.grammar_point: noun clauses (that-, wh- and whether-clauses as subject, object and complement)

listenings.text: Hi Mark. Last class you chose the verb that reported somebody else. Today you build the sentence that reports YOU, and the piece we need is a clause that behaves like a noun. Here is the idea. Anywhere you can put a noun, English lets you put a whole clause instead. The trouble is a fact. The trouble is that nobody agrees on a definition. Both sentences work, and the second one says infinitely more. That clause is doing the job of the word fact, and it can sit in three places. It can be the subject: what matters is the audience. It can be the object: I think that they deserve it. And it can come after the verb be, as the complement: the problem is whether the training counts. Now the traps, and there are three. The first is what. In Portuguese you would start with o que, and half my students write the what. In English it is just what, and that word is already the subject of its own clause, so you never add another one. The second trap is prepositions. After a preposition English wants what or whether, never that. It depends on what you call a sport. The question of whether it belongs in the Olympics. The third trap is that whether and if are not twins. Only whether survives after a preposition, before to, and at the front of a sentence. Whether it counts is debatable. Before class, write three sentences about anything you argued about this week, and start one of them with the word what. See you Monday, Mark.

Every few years somebody asks whether esports belong at the Olympic Games, and every few years the argument comes back in the same shape. So let me put my stance on the table first. What decides this is not whether the players sweat. That is the weakest test anybody has proposed, and shooting, sailing and archery have already survived it. What decides it is whether the thing being tested stays the same over time. A hundred meters in nineteen sixty is a hundred meters today, and that is why the record means something. A game is patched every three weeks. The version somebody wins on in July does not exist in October, and what that means is that the record has nowhere to live. Now, I will concede the strongest counterargument, because pretending it does not exist is how you lose a debate. The reasoning that the training is not real is simply false. That the top players practice ten hours a day is undeniable, that they have coaches and analysts and physiotherapists is documented, and anybody who calls it a hobby has not looked. So my assumption is not that these athletes are soft. My assumption is that the sport itself has to be stable enough to compare across generations, and that is where the evidence points the other way. What I would like is a separate competition with its own history. Whether anybody wants to hear that is another matter.

extra_audio.text: First, put your stance on the table in one sentence, because an argument that hides its conclusion is impossible to follow. Then give the strongest reason you have, and give it before the weak ones, since the second half of what you say is always heard less carefully. After that, name the evidence that supports the reason, so the listener can check you instead of trusting you. Next, concede the best counterargument in your opponent's own words, because doing it badly on purpose is the fastest way to lose the room. Finally, close by saying what matters most, so the last sentence is the one that carries your whole case.
